capability_schema_template_v1.0.intent: TEMPLATE — two to three sentences describing the evaluation goal and scoring philosophy. What will analysts learn by scoring vendors against this schema? Who is the audience? What decisions will the output inform? Example: 'Assess [MARKET] vendor capability depth across [N] pillars aligned to Gartner's [FRAMEWORK] framework. metadata.framework_alignment: TEMPLATE — list the external frameworks this schema aligns to (e.g., Gartner Market Guide 2025 + NIST CSF 2.0 + CIS Benchmarks + MITRE ATT&CK). Use this to anchor scoring criteria to recognized standards.

scoring_scale.meaning_of_zero: No publicly verifiable evidence of capability in this area
scoring_scale._note: The 0-5 scale below is the standard across all Gartner research schemas in this platform. Do not modify the scale values. Customize the descriptions only if this schema has a meaningfully different evidence bar (e.g., a services schema vs. a product capability schema).

scoring_logic.0: No Evidence: No publicly verifiable evidence of capability in this sub-pillar.
scoring_logic.1: Minimal: Basic or manual capability; limited automation, minimal technical specifics, or niche-only applicability.
scoring_logic.2: Generic Claims: Marketing mentions the capability but lacks named products, technical documentation, metrics, or meaningful specifics.
scoring_logic.3: Demonstrated: Documented capability with named products or features, some technical depth, identifiable use cases, and available customer validation.
scoring_logic.4: Advanced: Named products with measurable outcomes, analyst recognition, deep integration points, and automation-forward architecture.
scoring_logic.5: Market-Leading: Best-in-class capability with deep technical evidence, breadth across environments, analyst leadership recognition, measurable impact metrics, and continuous innovation. Reference customers and third-party validation available.

source_policy.description: Evidence must be publicly accessible and verifiable. Scores based on unverifiable internal briefings or analyst intuition alone should be flagged. Tier determines the evidence weight applied during quality review.

valid_sources._note: Tier A sources carry full weight — use these as the primary basis for scores of 3 or higher.

examples: Gartner Market Guide / Magic Quadrant / Hype Cycle

valid_sources._note: Tier B sources are valid corroborating evidence. Sufficient for scores up to 3-4 when multiple B sources agree.
Tier C sources alone are insufficient to justify scores above 2. Use only as supporting signals or for 0-1 scoring.

examples: Engineer-authored LinkedIn posts or blogs with technical detail

coverage_grade.description: Letter grade based on percentage of capability sub-pillars covered (score >= 1). Adjust the thresholds below to match your total sub-pillar count. The example thresholds assume approximately 20-30 sub-pillars total — recalibrate for significantly larger or smaller schemas.

vendor_type.TEMPLATE — Platform Vendor: TEMPLATE — Large platform vendors who deliver this capability as a deeply integrated component of a broader product suite.

pillars._note: Define 4-10 pillars. Each pillar is a major capability area evaluated by this schema. Pillar codes (keys) should be short uppercase abbreviations that will appear in the vendor table as column headers (e.g., CSPM, CWPP, CIEM). Use tier='core' for mandatory evaluation areas and tier='non-core (evaluate if present)' for differentiating capabilities that not all vendors will offer.

sub_pillars._note: Define 3-6 sub-pillars per pillar (total 15-40 sub-pillars is typical). Sub-pillar codes follow the pattern PILLARCODE-NN (e.g., PIL1-01, PIL1-02). Each sub-pillar scores a specific, narrow capability facet — precise enough that a researcher can determine the correct score from publicly available evidence in 15-30 minutes. Avoid overlapping definitions between sub-pillars in the same pillar.
